matter: Florida v. OpenAI and Sam Altman
description: The state alleges that OpenAI and its chief executive released and marketed ChatGPT, including to children, while hiding risks and ignoring internal safety warnings. It also alleges that ChatGPT collects minors' data without meaningful parental oversight, causes behavioral addiction and cognitive harm, and is prone to dangerous errors the company downplayed; the state seeks damages and an end to those practices, and on September 28, 2026 it asked the court for a temporary injunction.
topics: Chatbots and companions; Children and teens; Consumer protection and disclosure

description: The Justice Department and several states alleged that RealPage's rent-setting software used landlords' nonpublic, competitively sensitive data to set rents and had features meant to limit price cuts and align prices among competitors. A proposed consent judgment would bar the software from using competitors' nonpublic data to set rents, limit model training to nonpublic data at least 12 months old, require those features to be removed or redesigned, and add a court-appointed monitor. The case page also lists proposed judgments with five landlords; Greystar's is listed as final, dated March 2, 2026.

description: The Texas Attorney General alleged that Pieces Technologies, a Dallas company whose generative AI summarizes patients' conditions and treatment for hospital staff, made false and misleading claims about the accuracy and safety of its products, including a severe hallucination rate below 1 per 100,000. description: The FTC alleged that Rite Aid used AI facial recognition in its stores from 2012 to 2020 to spot suspected shoplifters, that it produced many false matches, and that the errors fell hardest on people of color. The proposed order would bar facial recognition surveillance for five years and require deleting the images and any algorithms built from them; the FTC's case page, last updated March 8, 2024, still lists it as pending.

description: The EEOC alleged that three integrated iTutorGroup companies programmed their tutor application software to automatically reject women aged 55 or older and men aged 60 or older, turning away more than 200 qualified U.S. applicants because of their age. The consent decree provides $365,000 for those applicants, training, a new anti-discrimination policy and injunctions against age and sex discrimination in hiring, and the EEOC will monitor compliance for at least five years.
topics: Hiring and work; Bias and automated decisions
